Present-kingdom writers answer that Revelation is arranged in cycles, so the order of the visions is not always the order of events; the final battle of 20:8-9 is the same battle as 19:19-21 and 16:14-16, all drawn from Ezekiel 38-39. If the nations were all destroyed in 19:21, there would be no nations left to deceive in 20:3. This is the only passage in the Bible that mentions a thousand-year reign, and it says nothing about Israel, Jerusalem as a capital, or the earth as the place of the reign; the thrones in Revelation are usually in heaven.

Future-kingdom writers reply that 19:21 speaks of the armies being killed, not every person on earth; survivors and their descendants make up the nations of the millennium. They argue that a doctrine does not need many verses if one clear text teaches it, and that Revelation 20 completes Old Testament promises of an earthly reign (Psalms 72:8; Zechariah 14:9). Historic premillennialists (Ladd, Blomberg) accept that the passage does not focus on Israel, but still read the order as chronological.
He reigns until the last enemy, then hands over the kingdom

In 1 Corinthians 15:23-26 Paul gives the order: Christ the firstfruits; then at his coming those who belong to him; then the end, when he hands the kingdom to the Father after abolishing every rule and power. He 'must reign until' all enemies are under his feet, and the last enemy destroyed is death. The present-kingdom reading holds that this reign runs from the resurrection to the return. Since death is destroyed when believers are raised at his coming (1 Corinthians 15:54-55), the reign ends at the return, which leaves no room for a later earthly reign in which people still die (as Isaiah 65:20 would require).

Premillennialists such as Ladd, Blaising and Storms (before his change of mind) argue that Paul's words 'then' (Greek epeita and eita) mark sequences with gaps: there are already two thousand years between 'Christ the firstfruits' and 'those who are his at his coming'. So there can also be an interval between his coming and 'the end'. In that interval, the millennium, Christ reigns and subdues his enemies, and death is destroyed at its close (Revelation 20:14).

Present-kingdom writers grant that eita can allow an interval, but argue that Paul's logic does not. Death is defeated when the dead in Christ are raised at his coming (verses 54-55); a millennium in which death continues would put the defeat of death a thousand years after the resurrection Paul ties it to. Sam Storms reports that this text was one reason he left premillennialism for amillennialism.
Psalms 2: the nations ruled with a rod of iron

Psalms 2 describes the nations raging, and God setting his king on Zion, his holy hill (Psalms 2:6), giving him the nations as an inheritance and the ends of the earth as his possession, to rule them with a rod of iron (Psalms 2:8-9). Revelation applies the rod of iron to Christ at his return (Revelation 19:15) and promises the same rule to faithful believers (Revelation 2:26-27). Future-kingdom writers argue that ruling nations with force only makes sense where rebellion still exists, which points to a reign over this present earth after the return, before the eternal state.

Present-kingdom writers answer that the New Testament applies Psalms 2 first to the resurrection: 'You are my Son, today I have begotten you' is fulfilled when God raised Jesus (Acts 13:33). Acts 4:25-28 applies the raging nations of Psalms 2:1-2 to Herod, Pilate and the Gentiles at the cross. Revelation 12:5 pictures the male child who will rule with a rod of iron being caught up to God's throne, which points to the ascension. The 'rod of iron' rule is exercised now by the risen king and finally in the last judgment.

Future-kingdom writers grant that Psalms 2 is partly fulfilled at the resurrection, but they argue that Revelation 2:26-27 and 19:15 still place the active rule of the nations in the future. They see the pattern of 'already' (enthronement) and 'not yet' (the nations actually subdued on earth) as pointing to a future earthly reign.
You have come to Mount Zion: receiving an unshakable kingdom

Hebrews 12:22-24 tells Jewish Christians that they have come (perfect tense) to Mount Zion, the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, to Jesus the mediator of a new covenant. Hebrews 12:26-28 then says God will shake heaven and earth once more so that only what cannot be shaken remains, and that believers are receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken. The present-kingdom reading holds that the Zion promises are being entered now by faith and will be completed in the final shaking, not in a rebuilt earthly Jerusalem. The writer also says Abraham himself looked for a city with foundations whose builder is God (Hebrews 11:10, 11:16).

Future-kingdom writers answer that the heavenly Jerusalem in Hebrews does not cancel the earthly one; it is the source of what will later come down (Revelation 21:2). Progressive dispensationalists see the new Jerusalem and a restored earthly Jerusalem as complementary stages. They also note that Hebrews was written to warn readers against going back to the temple system, not to address Israel's national future.

Present-kingdom writers reply that Hebrews deliberately contrasts the earthly Sinai and Jerusalem with the heavenly one (Hebrews 12:18-22; 13:14: 'here we have no lasting city'). The only shaking that remains is the final one, after which only the unshakable kingdom stays. That sequence leaves no room for a further earthly Jerusalem stage between the present and the final shaking.
Ezekiel 40-48: a detailed temple and land plan

Ezekiel 40-48 gives exact measurements for a temple, rules for priests from the line of Zadok, offerings, a prince, and new tribal borders for the land. Future-kingdom writers (Feinberg, Walvoord, Hullinger) argue that so much technical detail implies a literal fulfilment, and that it has never been fulfilled: the second temple did not follow this plan, and no river has flowed from the temple to heal the Dead Sea (Ezekiel 47:1-12). They place this temple in the millennium. Hullinger argues that the sacrifices there would cleanse ritual impurity in the presence of God, not take away sin, so they do not compete with the cross.

Present-kingdom writers (Block, Beale) answer that Ezekiel 40-48 is a vision, given on 'a very high mountain' (40:2), and is meant to show God's holy presence restored, not a building plan. Hebrews 10:12-18 says that where sins are forgiven there is no longer any offering for sin, and Ezekiel 45:17 and 45:20 use the language of atonement. The river of Ezekiel 47 is taken up in John 7:37-39 (the Spirit) and Revelation 22:1-2 (the river of life in the new Jerusalem), where John deliberately says there is no temple (Revelation 21:22).

Future-kingdom writers reply that Revelation 21:22 describes the eternal state, not the millennium, so it does not rule out a millennial temple. They argue that if Ezekiel's measured temple is only symbolic, then no amount of detail could ever indicate a literal meaning. Block, though not a dispensationalist, also sees the vision as tied to the land of Israel, which they say supports a concrete fulfilment.
Daniel 2: the stone kingdom set up in the days of those kings

Daniel 2:44 says that 'in the days of those kings' the God of heaven will set up a kingdom that will never be destroyed. In the dream the stone strikes the image in the time of the fourth kingdom, which most interpreters across camps identify as Rome. Jesus was born under Augustus, ministered and rose under Tiberius. The present-kingdom reading (e.g. E. J. Young) holds that the stone was cut out without hands in Christ's first coming, and that its growth into a mountain that fills the earth (Daniel 2:35) describes the spread of the kingdom through the gospel.

Dispensationalists (Walvoord) answer that the stone strikes the image on its feet and toes, which they see as a final, ten-part form of the fourth kingdom not yet seen in history. The stone destroys the empires suddenly and completely; it does not slowly replace them. So the stone is Christ at his second coming, setting up the millennial kingdom.

Present-kingdom writers reply that the text places the setting up of the kingdom in the days of 'those kings', not of a revived empire after a gap of two thousand years. They add that Daniel 7:13-14 shows the Son of Man receiving the kingdom by coming to the Ancient of Days, which the New Testament applies to the ascension (Acts 1:9; Matthew 26:64). Postmillennialists see the gradual growth of the mountain as exactly what the parables of the mustard seed and leaven describe (Matthew 13:31-33).
Matthew 23:39 and Luke 21:24: 'until'

Jesus tells Jerusalem that its house is left desolate and that they will not see him again 'until' they say, 'Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord' (Matthew 23:38-39). He also says Jerusalem will be trodden down by the Gentiles 'until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled' (Luke 21:24). Future-kingdom writers argue that 'until' marks a limit: the judgment on Jerusalem has an end, and it ends with the city welcoming its Messiah. This, they hold, points to a future national turning of Jerusalem's people to Christ at his return.

Present-kingdom writers answer that 'until' in Matthew 23:39 may state a condition rather than a promise: they will not see him until they welcome him, and only those who do so will see him with joy. Others grant a future turning of many Jews to Christ (Murray, Vos, Hodge) but deny that it brings a restored political kingdom. Luke 21:24 says the trampling has an end, but does not say what follows it is a national kingdom; Luke places the next event at the coming of the Son of Man (Luke 21:27).

Future-kingdom writers reply that even the conditional reading assumes that a future generation of Jerusalem will say the words, which still implies a national turning. They link this with Zechariah 12:10, where the house of David and the people of Jerusalem look on the one they pierced and mourn, a text John 19:37 and Revelation 1:7 apply to Christ.
The kingdom given to a nation producing its fruit

After the parable of the tenants, Jesus tells the chief priests and Pharisees that the kingdom of God will be taken from them and given to a nation (Greek ethnos) producing its fruits (Matthew 21:43). Peter later calls the church 'a holy nation' (1 Peter 2:9). The present-kingdom reading holds that this text does not say the kingdom is delayed for national Israel; it says the stewardship of the kingdom passes to a new people. This people is built on the Jewish apostles and the believing remnant of Israel, with Gentiles added.

Future-kingdom writers answer that the kingdom is taken from the leaders of that generation, not from Israel for ever. Vlach and Saucy argue that 'nation' may refer to a future, repentant generation of Israel that will produce the fruit, or to the church in the present age, without cancelling Israel's national promises. Romans 11:28-29 says the gifts and calling of God to Israel are irrevocable.

Present-kingdom writers note that Jesus speaks to the leaders as representatives of the vineyard's tenants, and that the vineyard is Israel (Isaiah 5:1-7). The kingdom passes to a fruit-bearing people, which in Matthew includes many from east and west who sit with Abraham (Matthew 8:11). They agree with Romans 11 that Jews remain beloved and may be grafted back in, but within this one people, not as a separate national kingdom.
Romans 11:26-29: an irrevocable calling

Paul says a partial hardening has come on Israel until the full number of the Gentiles has come in, 'and so all Israel will be saved' (Romans 11:25-26). He adds that, as regards election, they are beloved for the sake of the fathers, for the gifts and calling of God are irrevocable (Romans 11:28-29). Future-kingdom writers argue that 'Israel' in Romans 9-11 consistently means ethnic Israel, distinct from the Gentiles in the same sentence, and that God's irrevocable calling includes the national promises, among them the land and the throne. Horner and Vlach see this as the clearest New Testament proof that Israel's national future is still open.

Present-kingdom writers are divided here, which this study notes honestly. Some (Robertson, Wright, Holwerda) read 'all Israel' as the whole people of God, Jew and Gentile, or as the full number of the elect Jewish remnant through history. Others in the Reformed tradition (Murray, Vos, Hodge, and Moo outside it) expect a future large-scale turning of ethnic Jews to Christ. But all of them say that Romans 11 speaks of salvation by faith in Christ and being grafted back into the one olive tree, not of a restored political kingdom, a temple or a land.

Future-kingdom writers reply that the 'gifts and calling' must include the promises Paul himself lists in Romans 9:4 (the covenants, the giving of the law, the worship and the promises), which include the land. A future salvation of ethnic Israel, they argue, naturally brings with it the national blessings the prophets joined to it (Ezekiel 36:24-28). Ladd, a historic premillennialist, agreed on a future turning of Israel but did not build a separate national program on it.
Revelation 20 as a picture of the present age

Amillennialists read Revelation 20:1-6 as a new vision that goes back to the first coming of Christ (recapitulation), not as an event that follows chapter 19 in time. The binding of Satan so that he can no longer deceive the nations (Revelation 20:3) matches Jesus binding the strong man (Matthew 12:29), Satan falling (Luke 10:18), and the ruler of this world being cast out at the cross (John 12:31-32). The souls who reign with Christ are believers who have died and live with him now (Revelation 20:4); the 'first resurrection' is their entrance into life with Christ, as Meredith Kline argued. The thousand years is a symbolic number for the whole period between the comings.

Premillennialists (Ladd, Deere, Waymeyer) answer that Revelation 19:11-21 flows straight into 20:1, so the binding follows the return of Christ. The binding in Revelation 20 is total (Satan is thrown into a sealed pit), while the New Testament shows Satan still active now (1 Peter 5:8). They also argue that the same verb 'came to life' (ezesan) cannot mean a spiritual life in verse 4 and a bodily resurrection in verse 5 in the same passage.

Amillennialists reply that Revelation has clear recapitulation elsewhere (the final battle is described in 16:14-16, 19:19-21 and 20:8-9 with the same language from Ezekiel 38-39), so the battle of 20:8 is the battle of 19:19, not a second one a thousand years later. The binding is limited in purpose: Satan cannot stop the nations from hearing the gospel. On the verb, Kline and Riddlebarger argue that John contrasts two kinds of life and two kinds of death, matching 'first' and 'second' death.
The early church expected an earthly kingdom

Several of the earliest Christian writers held a future earthly reign of Christ. Papias, as quoted by Irenaeus (Against Heresies 5.33.3-4) and Eusebius (Church History 3.39.12), taught a thousand-year kingdom on the renewed earth. Justin Martyr says he and other fully orthodox Christians expect a resurrection and a thousand years in a rebuilt and enlarged Jerusalem (Dialogue with Trypho 80-81). Irenaeus devotes the end of Against Heresies (book 5, chapters 32-36) to a literal earthly kingdom in which the promises to Abraham are fulfilled. Future-kingdom writers argue that this is the oldest recorded Christian view, held close to the apostles.

Present-kingdom writers answer that chiliasm was never universal. Justin himself admits in Dialogue 80 that many Christians of pure and godly faith did not share it. Eusebius thought Papias was a man of very limited understanding who took apostolic figures too literally. Origen (First Principles 2.11.2) criticised readers who expected bodily pleasures in an earthly Jerusalem. Augustine says in City of God 20.7 that he once held a form of the view, then gave it up, and in 20.9 he teaches that the church is now the kingdom of Christ. The Nicene Creed (381) confesses that Christ's kingdom 'shall have no end'.

Future-kingdom writers reply that Justin's admission shows diversity, not that chiliasm was a minority view, and that the earliest witnesses (Papias, Justin, Irenaeus, Tertullian) are nearer the apostles than Origen or Augustine. They note that Augustine's influence, together with a Platonic dislike of the material world, explains the later decline of the view. Present-kingdom historians (Hill, Regnum Caelorum) answer that non-chiliast belief is also attested early, for example in 1 Clement and Polycarp.

God promises David that after his death he will raise up his offspring, who will build a house for God's name, and God will establish the throne of his kingdom for ever. God will be his father and he will be God's son. Solomon fulfilled this in part, but the words 'for ever' reach beyond him. Every later step in this line goes back to this covenant.

The psalm repeats the covenant as an oath: God has sworn to David that his offspring and throne will endure for all generations, and later that the throne will last 'like the sun' (Psalms 89:35-37). The same psalm then laments that the crown has been thrown to the ground (89:38-45), probably after the fall of Jerusalem in 587 BC. The promise and its apparent failure stand side by side and point forward to a greater son of David.

David hears the Lord say to 'my Lord': sit at my right hand until I make your enemies your footstool. The Davidic king is here seated beside God himself and is also a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek (110:4). Jesus uses this psalm to show that the Messiah is more than David's son (Matthew 22:41-45). It becomes the Old Testament text most often quoted in the New Testament.

A child will be born who is called Mighty God and Everlasting Father, and there will be no end to the increase of his government and peace on the throne of David. The Davidic king is now openly divine and his rule has no end. The present-kingdom reading sees the 'increase' as the growth of Christ's reign from his first coming onward; the future-kingdom reading sees its full form in the millennium.

Gabriel joins Isaiah 9 and 2 Samuel 7 in one announcement: God will give Mary's son the throne of his father David, he will reign over the house of Jacob for ever, and his kingdom will have no end. Both camps agree this identifies Jesus as the promised son of David. They differ on whether Luke means the throne to be taken at the ascension (as Acts 2 suggests) or also later in Jerusalem.

Peter says David died and was buried, so the psalm's promise was not about David himself. David, as a prophet who knew of God's oath to put a descendant on his throne, foresaw the resurrection. Jesus, raised and exalted to God's right hand, has fulfilled Psalms 110:1, and God has made him Lord and Christ. Here the throne of David and the right hand of God are joined; progressive dispensationalists (Bock) agree that a Davidic reign begins here, while classic dispensationalists see only a qualification for a future throne.

In Pisidian Antioch Paul tells Jews and God-fearers that the promise made to the fathers has been fulfilled for their children by raising Jesus. He quotes Psalms 2:7 ('You are my Son, today I have begotten you'), Isaiah 55:3 ('the holy and sure blessings of David') and Psalms 16:10. The Davidic sonship of 2 Samuel 7:14 is fulfilled in the resurrection, and the 'sure mercies' promised to David are now given to all who believe.

Paul describes the result of the enthronement: Christ is seated at God's right hand in the heavenly places, far above every ruler and authority, in this age and the age to come, with all things under his feet. This echoes Psalms 110:1 and Psalms 8:6. The Davidic king now reigns over the whole cosmos, and he is given as head over all things for the church.

Hebrews gathers the throne texts into one argument. After making purification for sins, the Son sat down at the right hand of the Majesty (1:3). The writer quotes Psalms 2:7 and 2 Samuel 7:14 (1:5), Psalms 45:6-7 ('your throne, O God, is for ever', 1:8-9), and Psalms 110:1 (1:13). The Davidic promise and the divine throne are fulfilled in the same exalted Son, now seated and waiting for his enemies to be made his footstool (10:12-13).

The risen Christ says he overcame and sat down with his Father on his throne, and that the one who overcomes will sit with him on his throne. Classic dispensationalists see two thrones here: the Father's throne now and Christ's own Davidic throne later. Present-kingdom writers answer that Revelation shows one throne of 'God and the Lamb' (Revelation 22:1, 22:3), so the Father's throne and the Messiah's throne are the same.

At the close of the Bible Jesus calls himself 'the root and the offspring of David, the bright morning star'. He is the source of David's line as well as its descendant (compare Isaiah 11:1, 11:10), and the star of Numbers 24:17. The line that began with the oath to David ends with the Davidic king reigning from the throne of God and the Lamb in the new Jerusalem, which both camps see as the final goal.

Romans 9-11 is Paul's sustained answer to the question: has God's word failed, since most of Israel has not believed in the Messiah? He answers in stages. Not all who are descended from Israel are Israel (Romans 9:6); God has always kept a remnant chosen by grace (Romans 11:5); Israel's stumbling has opened the door to the Gentiles, to provoke Israel to jealousy (Romans 11:11). Gentile believers are wild branches grafted into one olive tree and must not boast over the natural branches, which can be grafted in again if they do not continue in unbelief (Romans 11:17-24). Then Paul reveals a 'mystery': a partial hardening has come on Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, 'and so all Israel will be saved', as it is written that the Deliverer will come from Zion (Romans 11:25-27, citing Isaiah 59:20-21). He adds that Israel is an enemy regarding the gospel but beloved for the sake of the fathers, for God's gifts and calling are irrevocable (Romans 11:28-29). Who is 'all Israel', what does 'and so' (Greek kai houtōs) mean, and when does this salvation happen? Scholars in both families disagree, and the five readings below cut across the usual camp lines.
All Israel = the whole church of Jews and Gentiles

'All Israel' is the complete people of God, Jew and Gentile, the 'Israel of God' (Galatians 6:16). 'And so' means 'in this manner': by the hardening of part of Israel and the coming in of the Gentiles, the whole true Israel is saved. Nothing is said about a future era.
John Calvin (Commentary on Romans, 1540), N. T. Wright (The Climax of the Covenant, 1991; Paul and the Faithfulness of God, 2013), and some modern Reformed writers.

It fits Paul's redefinition of Israel in Romans 9:6 and the one olive tree of Romans 11:17-24. It reads 'and so' (houtōs) in its normal sense of manner rather than time. It agrees with Galatians 3:29 and Galatians 6:16.

In Romans 11:25 'Israel' clearly means ethnic Israel, which is partly hardened, distinct from the Gentiles; a sudden shift of meaning in the next verse seems unlikely to many. Paul's whole concern in Romans 9-11 is his kinsmen 'according to the flesh' (Romans 9:3). It also makes the 'mystery' less surprising, since Gentile inclusion was already known.
All Israel = the full number of elect Jews through history

'All Israel' is the total of the elect remnant of ethnic Jews, saved one by one throughout the age alongside the fullness of the Gentiles. 'And so' means 'in this way': through a remnant, never through the whole nation at once. The phrase is parallel to 'the fullness of the Gentiles'.
Herman Bavinck, Louis Berkhof, William Hendriksen, Anthony Hoekema, O. Palmer Robertson, Benjamin Merkle (JETS 2000).

It keeps 'Israel' ethnic throughout verses 25-26. It fits Paul's stress on the remnant in Romans 11:1-7, using himself as an example of a saved Jew in the present (Romans 11:1). It reads 'now' in Romans 11:31 (in many manuscripts, 'that they also may now receive mercy') as pointing to the present age.

Critics say it turns a climactic 'mystery' into something Paul had already said: that some Jews are saved. The contrast between 'in part' and 'all' (Romans 11:25-26) and between 'their trespass' and 'their fullness' (Romans 11:12) suggests a change in Israel's state, not merely its continuation.
A future large-scale conversion of ethnic Jews, without a national kingdom

After the fullness of the Gentiles, God will lift the hardening and bring the Jewish people as a whole (not every individual) to faith in Christ, probably near his return. They will be grafted back into the one olive tree, the church. No separate national kingdom or land program follows.

Charles Hodge, Geerhardus Vos, John Murray (Romans, NICNT, 1959-65), Douglas Moo (Romans, NICNT), Thomas Schreiner (Romans, BECNT), Kim Riddlebarger, and many Puritans and postmillennialists (Iain Murray, The Puritan Hope).

It keeps 'Israel' ethnic in verses 25-26 and gives full weight to 'mystery', 'until' and 'their fullness' (Romans 11:12, 15, 25). It explains Paul's hope that the natural branches will be grafted in again (Romans 11:23-24). It fits the Deliverer coming from Zion to turn ungodliness from Jacob (Romans 11:26).

Those who hold the elect-remnant view say Romans 11 never states a time sequence and that 'and so' is about manner, not 'and then'. Future-camp scholars say it stops short: if God keeps his word to ethnic Israel about salvation, why not also about the land and the nation that the same prophets promised?
National salvation leading to restoration in a millennial kingdom

At the second coming, after the tribulation, the surviving Jewish nation will turn to Jesus as Messiah (Zechariah 12:10). Then Israel will be restored as a nation in its land, and Christ will reign from Jerusalem in the millennium. Romans 11:29 shows that Israel's national election, including its land and covenant promises, is irrevocable.
John Walvoord, J. Dwight Pentecost, Charles Ryrie, Arnold Fruchtenbaum; progressive dispensationalists Craig Blaising, Darrell Bock and Michael Vlach (with more stress on Christ's present reign).

It reads 'Israel' ethnically throughout Romans 9-11 and takes 'the covenants' and 'the promises' of Romans 9:4 as still belonging to Israel. It connects Paul's citation of Isaiah 59:20 with the prophets' expectation of a restored nation. It treats 'irrevocable' (Romans 11:29) as covering the whole calling of Israel.

Romans 11 says nothing about the land, a millennium or a kingdom in Jerusalem; those elements are brought in from other texts. Paul's olive tree has one trunk, into which Jews are re-grafted, which seems to point to one people rather than two programs. Critics also note that in Romans 11:26 Paul changes Isaiah's 'to Zion' to 'from Zion', which some read as the heavenly Zion.
Historic premillennial: a future conversion at Christ's return, then the millennium

Ethnic Israel will turn to Christ in large numbers at or just before his return, when they see him (Matthew 23:39; Zechariah 12:10). They will enter the one people of God, not a separate program, and share in Christ's millennial reign on earth with the church.
George Eldon Ladd (A Theology of the New Testament, 1974; The Presence of the Future), Craig Blomberg, Barry Horner (a more national view), and many earlier premillennialists such as J. C. Ryle.

It joins the strengths of the future-conversion reading with a straightforward reading of Revelation 20. It ties Jesus' words 'you will not see me until you say, Blessed is he who comes' (Matthew 23:39) to Israel's future welcome of the Messiah. It avoids a strict two-peoples theology.

Amillennialists answer that Romans 11 gives no hint of a millennium after this conversion; Paul moves straight to doxology (Romans 11:33-36). Dispensationalists, on the other side, say it is inconsistent to read Romans 11 ethnically while reading the land promises typologically.
Which Testament has the last word?

The fulfilment family holds that the New Testament gives the final and authoritative sense of Old Testament promises. Jesus explained 'in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself' (Luke 24:27), and Peter says the prophets searched for the time of Christ's sufferings and glories (1 Peter 1:10-12). Later revelation does not contradict earlier promises, but it can show that they are fulfilled more fully than first readers could see.

The future family answers that the Old Testament must be read on its own terms first, because its first hearers were meant to understand it. Robert Saucy and Michael Vlach argue that the New Testament adds to Old Testament promises (for example, including Gentiles) but does not cancel or redefine what God promised to Israel. Otherwise, they say, the original promises would have misled their hearers.
Literal or typological fulfilment

Fulfilment scholars insist they read literally in the sense of 'as the author meant', but that the Bible itself uses types: Adam, David, the temple and the land point beyond themselves (Romans 5:14; Colossians 2:17). A type is a real thing in history that also foreshadows a greater reality. When the reality comes, the shadow is not restored but surpassed.

Dispensationalists such as Charles Ryrie call for consistent 'plain' or 'normal' interpretation of prophecy. They accept types, but deny that types cancel the original reference. Progressive dispensationalists speak of 'complementary' fulfilment: the church may share in a promise without removing its fulfilment for Israel.
The 'seed' of Abraham

Paul's argument in Galatians 3:16 that the promise was made to Abraham's 'seed', singular, that is, Christ, is decisive for the fulfilment reading. The promises narrow to one Israelite, then widen to everyone in him: 'if you are Christ's, then you are Abraham's seed' (Galatians 3:29). Physical descent alone never guaranteed the promise (Romans 9:6-8).
